modules.description: Fundamental concepts of electrocardiography and basic ECG interpretation

slides.title: What is an ECG?
slides.content: An electrocardiogram (ECG) is a medical test that measures the electrical activity of the heart. It provides crucial information about heart rhythm, rate, and potential abnormalities.

slides.title: ECG Lead System
slides.content: The standard 12-lead ECG system provides multiple views of the heart. Includes 6 limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) and 6 precordial leads (V1-V6).

quiz.question: How many leads are in a standard ECG?
quiz.explanation: A standard ECG uses 12 leads to provide comprehensive views of cardiac electrical activity.

slides.title: Normal Heart Rhythm
slides.content: Normal sinus rhythm characteristics: regular rhythm (60-100 bpm), P waves before each QRS, normal intervals, and consistent morphology.

quiz.question: What is the normal heart rate range for adults?
quiz.explanation: Normal resting heart rate for adults is typically 60-100 beats per minute.

modules.description: Understanding ECG waveforms, intervals, and their clinical significance

slides.title: P Wave Analysis
slides.content: The P wave represents atrial depolarization. Normal characteristics: duration <0.12s, amplitude <2.5mm, upright in leads I, II, aVF, V4-V6.

slides.title: QRS Complex
slides.content: QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization. Normal duration <0.12s. Q wave <0.04s and <25% of R wave amplitude.

quiz.question: What is the normal QRS duration?
quiz.explanation: Normal QRS duration is less than 0.12 seconds (3 small squares).

slides.title: T Wave and ST Segment
slides.content: T wave represents ventricular repolarization. ST segment should be isoelectric. ST elevation or depression indicates myocardial injury or ischemia.

quiz.question: What does ST elevation typically indicate?
quiz.explanation: ST elevation typically indicates myocardial injury, such as in acute myocardial infarction.

modules.description: Systematic approach to analyzing heart rate and rhythm patterns

slides.title: Rate Calculation Methods
slides.content: Three methods for rate calculation: 1) 300/R-R interval (large squares), 2) 1500/R-R interval (small squares), 3) Count R waves in 6 seconds × 10.

slides.title: Rhythm Regularity Assessment
slides.content: Assess rhythm regularity by measuring R-R intervals. Regular rhythm: variation <0.16s. Irregular rhythm: variation >0.16s.

quiz.question: How do you assess rhythm regularity?
quiz.explanation: Rhythm regularity is assessed by measuring R-R intervals between consecutive QRS complexes.

slides.title: Systematic Rhythm Analysis
slides.content: Systematic approach: 1) Rate, 2) Regularity, 3) P waves present?, 4) PR interval, 5) QRS duration, 6) Overall interpretation.

quiz.question: What is the first step in systematic rhythm analysis?
quiz.explanation: Rate calculation is the first step in systematic ECG rhythm analysis.

modules.description: Recognition and interpretation of common atrial arrhythmias

slides.title: Atrial Fibrillation
slides.content: Atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular rhythm, absent P waves, fibrillatory waves, variable R-R intervals. Risk of thromboembolism.

slides.title: Atrial Flutter
slides.content: Atrial flutter: sawtooth pattern (flutter waves), regular atrial rate ~300 bpm, variable ventricular response.

quiz.question: What is the characteristic pattern of atrial flutter?
quiz.explanation: Atrial flutter is characterized by a sawtooth pattern of flutter waves.

slides.title: Atrial Tachycardia
slides.content: Atrial tachycardia: regular rhythm, P waves present but abnormal morphology, rate >100 bpm, 1:1 AV conduction.

quiz.question: What distinguishes atrial tachycardia from sinus tachycardia?
quiz.explanation: Atrial tachycardia has abnormal P wave morphology compared to normal sinus P waves.

modules.description: Identification and clinical significance of ventricular arrhythmias

slides.title: Ventricular Tachycardia
slides.content: Ventricular tachycardia: wide QRS complexes (>0.12s), rate >100 bpm, regular rhythm, no P waves, hemodynamic instability possible.

slides.title: Ventricular Fibrillation
slides.content: Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic, irregular rhythm, no identifiable QRS complexes, immediately life-threatening, requires defibrillation.

quiz.question: What is the immediate treatment for ventricular fibrillation?
quiz.explanation: Ventricular fibrillation requires immediate defibrillation as it is immediately life-threatening.

slides.title: Premature Ventricular Contractions
slides.content: PVCs: wide QRS complexes, abnormal morphology, compensatory pause, may be benign or indicate underlying heart disease.

quiz.question: What characterizes a premature ventricular contraction?
quiz.explanation: PVCs are characterized by wide QRS complexes due to abnormal ventricular conduction.

modules.description: Understanding AV blocks and conduction abnormalities

slides.title: First-Degree AV Block
slides.content: First-degree AV block: PR interval >0.20s, every P wave followed by QRS, benign condition, may be normal variant.

slides.title: Second-Degree AV Block Type I
slides.content: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation until P wave blocked, usually benign, located in AV node.

quiz.question: What characterizes Mobitz Type I block?
quiz.explanation: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) is characterized by progressive PR interval prolongation until a P wave is blocked.

slides.title: Third-Degree AV Block
slides.content: Complete heart block: no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes, ventricular escape rhythm, may require pacemaker.

quiz.question: What is the hallmark of third-degree AV block?
quiz.explanation: Third-degree AV block shows complete dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity.
